claims.text: As-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type films contain local compositional inhomogeneities.
As-deposited FeMnNiGeSi-type films contain microstructural defects concentrated especially at grain boundaries.
Local compositional inhomogeneities and grain-boundary defects act as pinning centers for the magnetostructural transition.
Pinning by spatial inhomogeneity disorders and broadens the magnetostructural transition.
Spatial inhomogeneity causes hysteresis during low-field magnetocaloric cycling.
The as-deposited films have a nominal single-phase ordered hexagonal structure.
Post-deposition annealing just below the onset of the magnetostructural transition will promote chemical homogenization.
Post-deposition annealing will reduce defect density.
An inert annealing atmosphere will prevent oxidation.
There is an annealing-temperature window that enables atomic diffusion without significant phase decomposition or grain growth.
Reducing grain-boundary compositional variance and associated defects will produce a sharper magnetostructural transition.
Reducing grain-boundary compositional variance and associated defects will reduce transition hysteresis.
Annealed samples will have a narrower transition-temperature range than the as-deposited baseline.
Annealed samples will exhibit less hysteresis during magnetic-field cycling than the as-deposited baseline.
Annealing may enhance the peak magnetocaloric entropy change by making the phase transformation more uniform.
Previous studies of arc-melted ingots and melt-spun microribbons showed a sharp, hysteretic, first-order magnetostructural transition.
The predictions apply only while the non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type alloy retains the ordered hexagonal phase under low applied fields.
Annealing-induced grain growth or phase segregation may invalidate the predicted response.
Intrinsic electronic or magnetic coupling may contribute to hysteresis at a level comparable to microstructural inhomogeneity.
Failure of annealing to notably reduce hysteresis or narrow the transition-temperature range would falsify the proposed governing role of microstructural inhomogeneity.
